Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Reginald "Reg" Thompson's life took a drastic turn on a rainy evening three years ago. The 54-year-old interior designer was driving home from a meeting with a potential client when his car hydroplaned on the slick highway and spun out of control. Reg's memories of the accident are fragmented, but he recalls feeling weightless as his vehicle careened into a concrete median, crumpling the hood and sending shattered glass flying everywhere. Time seemed to slow down as he watched in horror, unable to move or escape the wreckage. The weeks that followed were a blur of surgeries, hospital stays, and physical therapy sessions. Reg's body had suffered extensive injuries – broken ribs, a punctured lung, and a severely damaged left leg that would require multiple operations to repair. As he slowly began to rebuild his strength, Reg started to notice strange and unsettling reactions to everyday stimuli. The sound of screeching tires or crunching metal made him jump, transporting him back to the moment of impact. He found himself avoiding driving whenever possible, opting instead for public transportation or ride-sharing services. At work, Reg's creativity began to suffer as he struggled to concentrate on design projects. His clients' requests seemed mundane and uninspiring compared to the constant din of "what-ifs" that echoed in his mind. What if another accident happened? What if his body failed him again? He started to doubt his own abilities, feeling like an imposter in a field where he had once excelled. Reg's self-doubt seeped into other areas of his life as well; he felt disconnected from friends and family, unsure of how to explain the emotional turmoil brewing inside him. Reg's divorce from his wife, Karen, two years prior had left him feeling unmoored, but this new sense of uncertainty was different. He couldn't shake the notion that he'd lost a fundamental part of himself in the accident – a part he might never regain. Simple tasks like walking or taking a shower became daunting challenges as Reg's mind insisted on conjuring worst-case scenarios. His body felt fragile and unreliable, as if it might betray him at any moment. As the months went by, Reg's avoidance behaviors took their toll. He stopped attending social gatherings, fearing that someone would ask about his accident or show sympathy – sentiments he couldn't bear to confront. At work, Reg began to delegate tasks more frequently, citing fatigue and stress as excuses for not taking on new projects himself. His business suffered as a result, and Reg found himself withdrawing further into his own world. It wasn't until Reg received an invitation to design the interior of a new rehabilitation center – one specifically catering to accident survivors like himself – that he began to realize just how much his life had changed for the worse. The irony was not lost on him: here was an opportunity to help others heal, yet he couldn't even begin to address his own emotional wounds. Reg felt trapped by his memories and fears, unable to trust his body or regain a sense of purpose. This realization, coupled with the weight of his accumulated losses – professional, social, and personal – finally prompted Reg to seek help. He began attending therapy sessions, hoping to learn how to quiet the cacophony of negative thoughts that had taken over his life. As he sat in the therapist's office for the first time, Reg couldn't help but wonder: would he ever be able to trust himself again?
